The Southern lake clam Diplodon chilensis attains a remarkable maximum shell length of 8.2 centimeters [Li = 8.2 centimeters], placing it among the larger freshwater bivalves native to the temperate lakes of southern South America. This ultimate total length, recorded from older individuals in stable lacustrine habitats, reflects a growth trajectory that slows considerably after the onset of reproductive maturity. Field surveys indicate that the total length at puberty for this species is approximately 2.15 centimeters [Lp = approximately 2.15 centimeters], a size typically reached within the first few years of benthic life. At this size, the developing gonads become histologically distinguishable, marking the transition from the juvenile stage to a reproductively competent sub-adult. The relatively small size at maturation compared to the final adult length suggests a life history strategy where reproductive activity commences well before somatic growth ceases, a pattern observed in many long-lived unionid and hyriid bivalves inhabiting oligotrophic environments.

Reproduction in Diplodon chilensis is characterized by the release of specialized parasitic larvae known as glochidia. At birth, each glochidium possesses a wet weight of just 0.000007 grams [Wwb = 0.000007 grams], representing an extremely minimal initial mass that is typical for bivalves producing large numbers of offspring. This minuscule birth mass is tied to the lecithotrophic larval phase, during which the glochidium relies entirely on stored yolk reserves and must rapidly attach to the gills or fins of a suitable fish host to continue development. The low wet weight at birth of 0.000007 grams [Wwb = 0.000007 grams] imposes a critical constraint on the larval energy budget, limiting the time window available for host encounter before endogenous reserves are exhausted. Successful metamorphosis on the host then triggers the transition to the free-living juvenile stage, which subsequently settles into the soft sediments of lake bottoms, beginning the slow process of somatic growth.

Maximum reproductive output in this species has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, the maximum daily reproduction rate translates to approximately 46.6 offspring per brood [N_R_i = approximately 46.6 offspring per brood] released in approximately one brood per day [F_R_i = approximately one brood per day], a figure derived from long-term observations of gravid individuals in experimental aquaria. This comparatively high daily fecundity compensates for the substantial mortality incurred during the parasitic larval phase, where only a small fraction of released glochidia successfully encounter a compatible host fish. The reproductive effort is sustained over several months during the austral spring and summer, with individual clams releasing broods in a series of pulses. The 11 °C [T = 11 °C] thermal regime is representative of the mean annual temperature in the deep, well-oxygenated waters of the species' native Patagonian lake habitats.

The ultimate flesh wet weight attained by a fully grown adult Diplodon chilensis has been estimated at 12.35 grams [Wwi = 12.35 grams], a value that reflects the substantial soft-tissue biomass accumulated over decades of filter feeding. This asymptotic flesh mass is reached only after the shell has approached its maximum length of 8.2 centimeters [Li = 8.2 centimeters], indicating that tissue growth continues to increase gradually even as longitudinal shell extension slows. The relatively modest flesh weight compared to the shell mass is characteristic of freshwater bivalves that allocate significant resources to a thick, protective calcium carbonate shell as a defense against predators such as muskrats and large crayfish. Seasonal fluctuations in body condition, tied to phytoplankton blooms and gonadal development, can temporarily alter the wet weight, but the long-term asymptotic value remains a stable species-level trait for populations in productive lacustrine environments.

Longevity in Diplodon chilensis is exceptional among freshwater bivalves of similar size, with a documented maximum lifespan of 73 years [am = 73 years] when individuals are maintained at an ambient temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. This extreme lifespan, recorded from mark-recapture studies in a protected Chilean lake, places the species among the most long-lived members of the Hyriidae family. The slow pace of life, characterized by delayed reproduction starting at a shell length of approximately 2.15 centimeters [Lp = approximately 2.15 centimeters], a modest daily reproductive output of roughly 46.6 offspring per brood [N_R_i = roughly 46.6 offspring per brood] released in about one brood per day [F_R_i = about one brood per day], and a minimal birth mass near 0.000007 grams [Wwb = 0.000007 grams], collectively supports a life history strategy oriented toward persistence in a stable but low-productivity environment. The slow accumulation of flesh mass to an ultimate value of 12.35 grams [Wwi = 12.35 grams] over such an extended lifetime underscores the exceptionally low metabolic costs and high survival rates that characterize this ancient lineage.
